title: Exposure to low-credibility online health content is limited and is concentrated among older adults: Evidence from linked survey and digital trace data
screen_reason: Linked survey and web/YouTube trace data from a national U.S. YouGov Pulse panel (N=1,059, ~4 weeks of browsing, Oct-Dec 2023). Reports behavioural REACH (13% of respondents visited at least one low-credibility health site; 9% saw such content on YouTube), EXPOSURE as a share of consumption (about 3% of health visits; about 10% of YouTube health views), per-capita intensity, explicit CONCENTRATION (top 1% of users = 37% of exposure; top 10% = 77%), and a source-level CONTENT share (78/1,155 health domains coded low-credibility). All have stated denominators.

estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who viewed at least one low-credibility health video on YouTube in a ~4-week window
estimates.value_raw: 0.09 (95% CI 0.07-0.12); "About 9% saw this sort of content (95% CI: 7-12%)"
estimates.denominator: 1,059 U.S. adult panellists with logged trace data (76% of whom visited YouTube at least once), survey-weighted
estimates.definition: Respondent counted if at least one of the YouTube videos they played was labelled low-credibility health content by the hybrid human/GPT-4o credibility coding.
estimates.misinfo_def: Health-information credibility assessed with 'a structured code book designed to assess health information credibility' (Appendix A); the paper's overall frame is 'low-credibility health content' rather than verified falsehood.
estimates.source_quote: About 9% saw this sort of content (95% CI: 7-12%).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Older adults consume less YouTube health content overall, but a higher proportion of it is low-credibility'; Table D.26
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two-stage hybrid: 3,902 health-related videos identified by embedding classification (human validation Cohen's kappa 0.92 between coders, 0.93 human vs automated); 400 randomly sampled videos manually coded with a structured credibility codebook, then a GPT-4o model given the codebook and all 400 labelled examples classified the remaining 3,502; human validation coders agreed with each other at kappa 0.97 and with the model at kappa 0.89, and all discrepant cases were manually corrected to the human codes.
estimates.moderator_quote: During data collection, 76% of respondents visited YouTube at least once. Beginning with a corpus of over 470,000 YouTube videos viewed in our sample, we used the same embedding-based classification technique described above to label each video as health-related (1) or not health-related (0).
estimates.notes: REACH → denom_scope population. Denominator is the whole panel, not only YouTube users, so the 9% is diluted by the 24% who never opened YouTube. breadth coded misleading because 'low-credibility' is a credibility-codebook judgement of the video, not a verified false claim.

estimates.platform: Websites (health domains observed in panel browsing)
estimates.date: Domains observed in the ~4-week browsing window, October-December 2023
estimates.measure_type: % of health-tagged website domains visited by the panel that were hand-coded low-credibility
estimates.denominator: 1,155 unique domains carrying a 'Health' category tag in the panel's 9.7m logged web addresses (89,562 unique parent-level domains overall)
estimates.definition: A domain was coded low-credibility if it included inaccurate or misleading health information, existed primarily to sell products with unverified claims, was flagged deceptive/untrustworthy by the browser, or carried content lacking sources or apparently LLM-generated.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Primary criteria were site including inaccurate or misleading health information, site focusing primarily on sales products featuring unverified claims, site indicated as \"deceptive,\" \"untrustworthy,\" or similar by web browser, or site featuring content that primarily lacked sources, links to credible sites, or appeared to be generated by large language models."
estimates.source_quote: Of the 1,155 domains with a health category tag, only 78 (6.8%) were manually determined to be low-credibility.
estimates.page_loc: Online Methods, 'Digital trace data: Web'; repeated in Appendix A 'Low-credibility domain'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two coders assessed all health-tagged domains on the domain string alone; Krippendorff's alpha = 1.00 for the credibility label and .92 for the 'Sales' sub-code. The Lasser et al. compiled list was rejected as inadequate (only 48/1,154 health domains appeared on it, 39 of them rated credible).
estimates.moderator_quote: There are a total of 45,395 URLs with a "health" value of 1 (compared with 9,895,086 URLs with a "health" value of 0).
estimates.notes: Borderline: this is a supply-side count of DISTINCT DOMAINS in the panel's browsing, each counted once regardless of traffic, so it is not a share of content people saw (that is the 3% exposure row). Kept as CONTENT because the denominator is all health domains that exist in the corpus. Note the paper twice gives the health-domain denominator slightly differently (1,155 in the main text, 1,154 'private domains' in Appendix A).

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Age-group breakdowns (60+ vs 18-29 exposure, ideology and right-leaning-news interactions) are regression coefficients and jittered scatter plots, not shares with denominators, so no subgroup rows — and the age gradient, though the paper's headline, is reported as b/SE, not as a percentage per age group. 2) 'about 77% of our sample saw health content' and '35% ... saw some health content [on YouTube]' are denominators for the ratio rows, not misinformation prevalences, so no separate rows. 3) Referral shares (Figure 3 / Table D.16: traffic to low-credibility sites coming from other low-credibility sites rather than search or social) are counts of referral events per respondent shown only in figures; no numeric share is printed in the text I have. 4) The combined web+YouTube exposure measure (Table D.35) is reported only as regression output, no headline share. 5) 'only 48 (4%)' of health domains appeared on the Lasser dubious-news list and 39/48 of those were rated credible — an instrument-comparison figure, not a prevalence. 6) 'over 90% of such [untrustworthy political] articles were pro-Trump' is cited from Guess et al. 2020, not this study. 7) Survey-based measures (cancer headline discernment, cancer risk-factor misperceptions) are BELIEF measures, excluded by the protocol. 8) Table D.1 gives the binary health-exposure mean as 0.74 while the text says 'about 77%'; noted on the relevant row, and it does not affect the extracted low-credibility values. QUOTE FORM: the text file is a line-numbered manuscript, so every sentence is broken by a stray line-number line; each source_quote is therefore the exact within-line span carrying the value. Row 0's sentence continues '10-15%)' after the break, and row 2's continues 'visits to such sites (SD = 3.14, max = 122)'.

rob.design: Linked survey + passive-metering panel study. Survey N = 1,200 fielded by YouGov 25 Oct - 21 Nov 2023, respondents matched and weighted to approximate U.S. population demographics; N = 1,059 logged web visits and form the analytic sample (opt-in Pulse Panel with RealityMine metering across mobile, tablet and desktop). Trace corpus: 9.7m web addresses, 1.9m unique addresses, 89,562 parent domains, ~4 weeks per respondent (2 weeks each side of the survey), plus 470,000+ YouTube video plays. Health tagging via provider category tags plus an OpenAI text-embedding model, validated on a stratified sample of 300 URLs (97% true positive rate; human-vs-automated Cohen's kappa 0.96). Low-credibility health domains hand-coded by two coders, Krippendorff's alpha 1.00 (sales sub-code .92); YouTube credibility coded by 400 manual labels plus GPT-4o classification of 3,502 videos, human-model kappa 0.89, discrepancies corrected to human codes. Pre-registered (OSF) with pre-specified covariates; descriptive statistics reported with survey weights. Stated limitations: no observation of exposure without a click-through, opt-in tracking panel, no causal identification, U.S. only. Respondents had also been randomised to media-literacy interventions analysed elsewhere; the authors show no treatment effects on downstream exposure (Table D.9).
rob.item6_quote: Of the 1,155 domains with a health category tag, only 78 (6.8%) were manually determined to be low-credibility. Primary criteria were site including inaccurate or misleading health information, site focusing primarily on sales products featuring unverified claims, site indicated as "deceptive," "untrustworthy," or similar by web browser, or site featuring content that primarily lacked sources, links to credible sites, or appeared to be generated by large language models.
rob.item10_quote: Over the data collection period (approximately 4 weeks per respondent), about 13% saw any URLs from these domains (95% CI: 10-15%). ... We find that about 77% of our sample saw health content during this period, averaging about 34 total health visits (SD = 77.21, max = 1,064). This means low-credibility visits are a small proportion of all health visits (roughly 3%).
